extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (design patent applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and evaluating U.S. design patent applications (35 U.S.C. 171) including ornamentality, novelty (35 U.S.C. 102), computer-generated icons, multiple-part designs, simulation, offensive subject matter, and evidence standards for rejections and rebuttals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-generated icon: article-of-manufacture requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the disclosure as a whole does not suggest or describe the claimed subject matter as a computer-generated icon embodied in a computer screen, monitor, other display panel, or portion thereof, reject the claimed design under 35 U.S.C. 171 for failing to comply with the article of manufacture requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disclosure does not support embodiment as an icon in a display, state that the claim is fatally defective under 35 U.S.C. 171; amendments attempting to overcome the rejection will ordinarily be entered but any new matter must be canceled (if new matter is added, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph). If the disclosure as a whole does suggest such embodiment, indicate that drawings may be amended to overcome the rejection and suggest amendments to bring the claim into compliance. Upon applicant reply, enter amendments and review the record; if by a preponderance of the evidence (In re Oetiker) applicant establishes the icon is embodied in a display, withdraw the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of type fonts
rubrics_metrics.description: Type fonts have historically been granted design patents; modern computer generation of fonts is not a basis to reject a type font design under 35 U.S.C. 171 for failure to be an article of manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject claims for type fonts under the article-of-manufacture requirement on the basis that modern typesetting no longer uses solid printing blocks; treat type fonts as eligible subject matter for design patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changeable (animated) computer-generated icons: claim requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-generated icons that change in appearance during viewing may be the subject of a design claim; such a claim may be shown in two or more views with images understood as viewed sequentially and no ornamental aspects attributed to the transitional process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a descriptive statement in the specification describing the transitional nature and making clear the claim does not include anything not shown. Example statements are provided (e.g., 'The subject matter in this patent includes a process or period in which an image changes into another image. This process or period forms no part of the claimed design.'). The process/period of transition is not part of the claimed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designs comprising multiple articles or multiple parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed design may encompass multiple articles or multiple parts within an article, but the title must identify a single entity of manufacture made up by the parts (e.g., set, pair, combination, unit, assembly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a descriptive statement in the specification clarifying the claim is directed to the collective appearance. If separate parts are shown in a single view, show the parts embraced by a bracket '}'. For multiple parts of a single article: show the article in broken lines and various parts in solid lines (no bracket needed). See MPEP §1503.01 for further formal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamentality standard (definition and overall test)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ornamental feature/design is one 'created for the purpose of ornamenting' and is not merely a by-product of functional or mechanical considerations; to be patentable, a design must be 'primarily ornamental.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine ornamentality by viewing the claimed design in its entirety—the ultimate question is whether the overall appearance is dictated by utilitarian purpose or created for ornament. Consider purposes of particular elements, but assess overall appearance. Distinguish functionality of the article from functionality of the specific design feature. Case law examples (In re Carletti; L.A. Gear; Norco) and tests are cited to guide the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie evidence requirements for lack of ornamentality
rubrics_metrics.description: To properly reject a claimed design under 35 U.S.C. 171 for lack of ornamentality, the examiner must make a prima facie showing and provide a sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper evidentiary bases include evaluation of the appearance of the design itself, the examiner's knowledge of the art, a reply to a letter of inquiry, a brochure emphasizing functional/mechanical features, the specification of an analogous utility patent, or information in the application. Examiners must detail and support assertions, especially when an article has general use. Examples of acceptable evidence: (A) common knowledge in the art; (B) appearance of the design; (C) specification of a related utility patent; (D) information provided in the specification. Rejections should not be made absent such evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of lack-of-ornamentality rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 171 for lack of ornamentality based on a proper prima facie showing fall into two categories: (A) a design visible in its ultimate end use which is primarily functional based on the evidence of record; or (B) a design not visible in its normal and intended use such that its appearance is not a matter of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case law (In re Stevens; In re Webb) to support the category selection and ensure the evidentiary basis corresponds to the category asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shifting and applicant rebuttal standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the examiner establishes a proper prima facie case of lack of ornamentality, the burden shifts to the applicant to come forward with evidence or argument to rebut the rejection; attorney arguments are not a substitute for evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may submit affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 from the applicant or a company representative explaining ornamental considerations and identifying aspects of the design that meet those considerations. Examiner may use form paragraphs (e.g., 15.08, 15.08.01). Case law (In re Oetiker; Ex parte Webb) requires factual evidence rather than lawyer argument. Applicant evidence may include sworn statements, advertisements, sales literature, customer declarations, or other documentary proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 15.08 requirements (lack of ornamentality — visible in end use)
rubrics_metrics.description: ¶ 15.08: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 171 as lacking ornamentality; the following evidence establishes a prima facie case of lack of ornamentality and evidence to demonstrate ornamentality may be submitted as an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavit/declaration should (a) state the ornamental considerations which entered into the design, and (b) identify what aspects of the design meet those considerations. Examiner Note: insert source of evidence of lack of ornamentality (e.g., utility patent, brochure). Attorney arguments are not an adequate substitute for evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 15.08.01 requirements (lack of ornamentality — not visible in normal use)
rubrics_metrics.description: ¶ 15.08.01: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 171 when the design appears to have no period in commercial life when its ornamentality may be a matter of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To overcome, applicant needs two types of evidence: (1) evidence there is some period in the commercial life when ornamentality is a matter of concern (e.g., sales literature, advertisement, catalog), and (2) evidence that the design is ornamental (CFR 1.132 affidavit identifying 'thought of ornament'). Company representative declarations are acceptable. Examiner Notes: insert name of article and source of evidence. Attorney argument insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming lack-of-ornamentality rejection — permissible evidence types
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 based on lack of ornamentality may be overcome by specified kinds of evidence and explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable rebuttal evidence includes: (A) affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 explaining which features were created to enhance saleable value or for esthetic appearance; (B) advertisements emphasizing ornamentality; (C) evidence of distinctness from prior art or efforts to maintain consumer recognition; (D) company representative statements showing motivating factors; (E) evidence of alternative designs that could have served the same function (to show appearance not dictated by function); (F) evidence establishing visibility/period in commercial life when ornamentality matters (In re Webb). Attorney argument alone is insufficient. Cite relevant cases (Gorham; Berry Sterling; L.A. Gear; Webb) as guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of evidence submitted to overcome rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must evaluate applicant-submitted evidence in light of the design as a whole to decide if the claim is primarily ornamental; mere display at trade shows or inclusion in catalogs is insufficient by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must show the design was created for the 'purpose of ornamenting' (In re Carletti). Evidence must provide clear and specific indication of ornamentality to be probative (Berry Sterling). When visibility during end use is at issue, applicant must show the article's design is a 'matter of concern' during some period between manufacture/assembly and ultimate use (In re Webb). Declarations from customers/users attesting ornamentality during commercial life are appropriate. Applicants not directly involved in sales/users cannot generally provide factual evidence about purchase reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility requirement for designs hidden in end use
rubrics_metrics.description: When a design would be hidden during its ultimate end use, the requirements for visibility of the design and proof it was created for the 'purpose of ornamenting' must both be met to overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must show a period in the commercial life when ornamentality is a matter of concern; mere possibility of making a concealed element visible (e.g., by encasing in transparent cover) is insufficient. Cite Norco Products v. Mecca and In re Webb guidance; examiner should require concrete evidence of a visibility period and ornament-driven design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation/originality standard
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 171 requires a design to be 'original'; a design that simulates an existing object or person (natural form without stylistic departure) is not original and should be rejected as nonstatutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject claims directed to simulations of well-known or naturally occurring objects/persons under 35 U.S.C. 171 (use form paragraphs 15.08.02 and 15.08.03). Where possible, provide evidence of the appearance of the object/person being simulated so a comparison can be made. If prior art anticipates or renders the claim obvious, concurrently reject under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103(a). Case examples: Gorham, In re Smith, Bennage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive subject matter prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Design applications disclosing subject matter that could be deemed offensive to any race, religion, sex, ethnic group, or nationality (e.g., caricatures or depictions) should be rejected as nonstatutory subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 171.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such subject matter also violates 37 CFR 1.3 (presentation lacking decorum and courtesy). Use Form paragraph 15.10 to reject. Cite MPEP § 608 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty standard for design patents (35 U.S.C. 102 and average observer test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102 requires that the claimed design not have been known or described in the prior art; the relevant test is the 'average observer' test — whether the average observer takes the new design for a different, not a modified, already-existing design. The reference must be identical in all material respects to anticipate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The average observer test does not require analogous arts; the observer is not charged with knowledge of any art. Functional and/or hidden features may not be relied upon to support patentability in a 102 rejection. Differences in functional considerations alone do not negate anticipation. Case law: In re Barrlett/Barlett (quoting Shoemaker), Hupp v. Siroflex, In re Glavas, In re Cornwall, Black & Decker v. Pittway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception and statutory bars (design patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental use exception to public use/sale bars under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) usually does not apply to design patents, though there are limited cases involving experimentation of functional features that may negate public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Mann (experimental use usually not applicable to designs) and Tone Brothers v. Sysco (experimentation on functional features in a product that also contains an ornamental design may negate public use). Examiner should evaluate statutory bar issues under MPEP §2133.03(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign priority and 35 U.S.C. 102(d) for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration of a design abroad is treated as equivalent to patenting for 35 U.S.C. 102(d) purposes; a U.S. design application must be filed within six months of the foreign filing to claim priority (35 U.S.C. 172 modifies 102(d) for designs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the foreign protection vests (registration/grant) and the U.S. application is timely filed (within 6 months), priority will vest; otherwise a statutory bar arises. The MPEP provides a table of countries and the foreign dates usable for 35 U.S.C. 102(d) purposes (varies by country — e.g., date of registration, publication, filing date, etc.). See MPEP §1504.10 for details.
